utterances.text: It was agreed that General Kukanjac should leave the command building on his own, that he should go to Lukavica and order a ceasefire by the JNA. At the same time it was agreed that Izetbegovic would be off to the Presidency building to order a cease-fire to the other side, the Muslim side. As a matter of principle, Kukanjac accepted this agreement. He designated he to stand-in for him once he was out of the command building. Nevertheless, I had my own condition to impose. I wanted three UNPROFOR men to stay with me back at the command building. I knew that the crowd laying siege to the building would eventually be launching an attack. General Kukanjac accepted that and told Aksentijevic, "Go see Ganic and make that proposal." Aksentijevic left, and as we were waiting for him to come back, we used our Motorolas and radio communication to find out who was ordering the Muslim forces to kill Kukanjac and at any cost prevent him from reaching Lukavac -- Lukavica alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was Izetbegovic at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Still at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: For this reason, Kukanjac gave up the plan. We were waiting for Aksentijevic. Aksentijevic came back and told us - and I was there too when he said this - that Ganic had refused the plan. Ganic wanted to see his first request acknowledged and complied with. He said, "Kukanjac has no place being there. You're all captives, prisoners, of the BH Presidency. Unless you do what we ask, we'll change tack in terms of what we do with you." Kukanjac interrupted his talks with Ganic and got in touch with Alija Izetbegovic. He resumed their previous conversation and Izetbegovic accepted all of his requests. He allowed 20 trucks to leave Lukavica and be on their way to the 2nd Military District command building. We wanted to use these trucks to drive back to Lukavica. At his own initiative he came to see Kukanjac and offered verbal guarantees to the fact that the column would be allowed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "he," you mean Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Izetbegovic said, "My presence here guarantees that no one would be attacked. I have here with me the responsible commander who's offering the same guarantees."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Was anyone from UNPROFOR there at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General MacKenzie as well as those people from the international community, Mr. Santos as far as I remember. Kukanjac had ordered for the JNA to not fire at the column under any circumstances, even if we ourselves were to come under attack. Pursuant to the terms of the agreement, the column was headed by MacKenzie followed by an APC holding Kukanjac and Izetbegovic. In the third APC there was Izetbegovic's army commander. The convoy headed out. They were intercepted in Dobrovoljacka Street and were attacked from all sides. I was in the medical vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. In which vehicle were you in terms of the sequence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was vehicle number 11 or possibly number 10 if you look at the entire convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many men in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Eight, eight persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were stopped and the attackers opened all of the doors. They held us at gunpoint and took away our personal weapons. I saw them driving the JNA men out of those vehicles behind us. They were taking away their weapons, taking away some of their clothes, hitting them with rifle-butts, knocking them onto the ground, and pressing their necks down with their boots, as well as firing shots. They ordered us to leave the medical vehicle and go out, which I refused. Another group arrived and one of those new men opened a burst of gun-fire from automatic rifle at Colonel Miro Sokic, an ethnic Croat who was seated to my right. The brain and the blood from his skull splattered all over my face. It was very difficult for me to cope with this stress. At the same time, there were other bursts of gun-fire killing Colonel Budimir Radulovic, who was on the front seat of that vehicle right next to the driver. I ordered the driver to go to the military hospital. We were off heading towards the head of the convoy. I saw General MacKenzie standing next to the second APC, just standing there, and there was this APC in which there were Izetbegovic and General Kukanjac. I saw Colonel Jovo Divjak right there, who was giving orders to the effect, "Stop shooting, stop shooting." I overheard conversations, but all I remember is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Who was Colonel Jovo Divjak at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Divjak was a JNA colonel assigned to the BH Territorial Defence. In 1991, because of a campaign of secretly arming a company of the HVO in the village of Doglodi, near Sarajevo, he was sentenced to eight months in prison by the military court in Sarajevo. We were awaiting a sentence from the supreme military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, but what was Jovo Divjak's position at the time, the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I read his accounts later in the media. He suggested that he was deputy commander of the TO staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We proceeded in our medical vehicle with no weapons and carrying some dead bodies. We proceeded on to the military hospital. At the crossroads between Skenderija and the hygiene institute, we were caught in a cross-fire from the right, the direction the vehicles were moving, the mosque area; and on the left there was the book shop neighbourhood. There was a cross-fire. I bent down near the floor. Fortunately, they missed the driver and we still managed to cross the crossroads and get past it quite quickly. We got closer to the hospital, got through the BH army blockade, and once we were inside we concluded that along the road between that place and the military hospital, when I stood back up I realised that a lady who was with the medical unit, a Muslim called Nurmela Sukro, was shot right through her head. In the middle of her forehead there was a bullet wound, and back at the military hospital they ascertained that Colonel Miro Sokic had also been killed as well as Colonel Budimir Radulovic and this lady, Nurmela Sukro. Seriously wounded, seven shots to the back. A private, lance corporal, Dragan Kovacevic, fortunately he was wearing -- he was wearing a flak jacket. And I myself had received a shot to the shoulder. I was wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I know it's very unpleasant for you to recount all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have another document from the 65 ter list, 00654D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I showed you this document in our proofing session. You've already mentioned a number of names during the course of your testimony. You don't have to mention them again. You can just tell us whether you know that some other people on this list were killed on the same day, on the 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the people that I mentioned, I know that Colonel Gradimir Petrovic, who was the chief of the technical service in the command of the 2nd Military District, he replaced me; and Colonel Bosko Mihajlovic were also killed on the asphalt road. They kept their boots on their necks, they stripped them to their underwear, and then they shot them in the back of the head. And I know some other people from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to what you knew at the time and what you learned later, would the number of 29 persons on the list reflect the number of those who were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were 42 members of the JNA who were killed on the 2nd and 3rd of May in Sarajevo. That's the list that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many were captured during those incidents, how many members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember according to the data that I subsequently saw, about 160 or 190, I can't remember exactly, were captured or taken prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D401. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, after the 2nd of May, how long did you remain in the territory of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From the 3rd of May, 1992, until the 8th of May, 1992, I was in the military hospital in Sarajevo. On the 8th of May I was discharged from the military hospital in Sarajevo and I joined a column headed by General MacKenzie. That column transported the wounded from the Kosevo Hospital as well as those heavily wounded who had been hospitalised in the Sarajevo military hospital. Since I knew MacKenzie from before and since General Kukanjac had told him to help me get out of the military hospital, I joined the convoy and I did leave Sarajevo with the convoy and I ended up in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Lukavica, do you know the date or do you know the approximate date when you left Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From Lukavica I phoned my family in the apartment in Sarajevo, and I learned that that family was in a private camp. I learned that on several occasions two MPs of the BH army had come to the apartment, they had searched the apartment, they had ill-treated the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to the witness giving that answer. The question is very simple. "How long did you stay in Lukavica, do you know the date or do you know the approximate date when you left ..." And now we're digressing into other elements that are not part of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection and I will instruct the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I will be asking you about different things that we discussed during the proofing session, but now I would kindly ask you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was: How long did you stay in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In Lukavica and occasionally at Pale and also occasionally at the Main Staff which had been set up, I stayed there and my main goal --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, we'll come to that. Just tell me, please, how long did you stay in Lukavica, up to what date? That was my question. And I will have other questions as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime up to the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. While you were in the territory of the city of Sarajevo and in the general territory - and you mentioned Pale and as far as I can see you also mentioned the base of the Main Staff which is Han Pijesak - and we will come to that, we will -- did you stay in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for some time and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed until the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reason? Why did you stay in the territory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The main reason was to try and save my family from the apartment in Sarajevo where they were held captives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now tell me, what information do you have? Who was there? What was their status? Who were your family members at the time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My wife and my 16-year-old daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what conditions did they live in at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The first problem was that around the building shells fell very often, and together with the other residents of the building they had to go to a private camp in the basement. The second problem was that they didn't have any food. The situation was very difficult. They didn't have food or water. On several occasions, two MPs of the BiH army military police came. They introduced themselves as policemen, and they allegedly told them, "Madam, you're a Serb, your husband is a Serb Chetnik, we can do with you whatever we want and we will not be held accountable for that." They wanted to take my daughter to a brothel in the atomic shelter in the same neighbourhood, and then they started -- both started screaming and shouting. And in the basement there was a Muslim lady who resided there and she would always try to prevent that from happening, and she would tell those two police officers that I, as their husband and father, was a good man. And she said, "I can't let the family of such a good man come to any harm." And that woman's husband worked in the institution that I -- that was under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just -- what does the acronym "MP" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the military police of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter used the acronym "MP," military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that your family told you that those were the men who came knocking on their door; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said that there were always two of them, two men in uniforms. And they introduced themselves and they said, "Madam, we are the BiH army police."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe the time is right for our next break unless you need any further clarifications of the issue that you raised, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Trial Chamber doesn't want to interfere with your examination, but it is nonetheless concerned about where we are going with all these questions because they don't seem to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that from this moment on we are going straight into the matter of our case; however, what we have been discussing so far is also relevant for our Defence case and we wanted to hear about this episode from the witness because it's very important for the position of the Defence. In any case, we are now moving on to the matters which go straight into the heart of the Defence case and the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, my question is this: In the following period, the period after that, did you again meet with General Kukanjac? That's my first question and then I'll have a few more after that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him once -- or rather, twice. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just -- when you say "following that period," can you give us a time-span what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I wanted to talk about the period when the General was in Lukavica, once he was discharged from the military hospital in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the first time I met General Kukanjac on the 19th or 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: And the second time, on the 3rd of May, 1993, when he organised the meeting of us who survived from the volunteers, and that meeting was organised in Belgrade, from Dobrovoljacka Street actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the first meeting. We heard the Army of Republika Srpska was established, and I'm now asking you about the 19th of May. How do you remember the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Because I learnt at the time that an order had been issued about the establishment of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, and in that order it said that all members of the former JNA who were born in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro were supposed to join the Army of Yugoslavia, which was then known as the SRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that you misspoke on page 59, line 9, when you said that the Army of Serbia and Montenegro was established.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke and I apologise for that. At that time a possibility was given to everybody, to all members of the JNA - and that was also an order for all members of the JNA who were under the command of the 2nd Military District - to leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and join the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was somebody else with Mr. Kukanjac when you saw him on the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Kukanjac came in a helicopter and General Mladic came with him in the same helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Did you talk to him on that occasion; if you did, what was the topic of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We entered a room, or rather, an office in the 4th Corps command in Lukavica. There were General Kukanjac, General Mladic, Colonel Gagovic, and myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Colonel Gagovic's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant commander for logistics in the 4th Corps. General Kukanjac wanted to see me, and when he saw me, when he saw that I was alive and well, albeit slightly wounded, he cried which was rather strange given the type of commander that he was. However, he was really glad and at the same time he was sorry about all these men who had been killed. And he said that. He said that he had been cheated that the authorities --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question that was asked to the witness was: What was Colonel Gagovic's position at the time, and again we seem to be expanding into a much broader answer than the question calls for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My previous question was, that is on page 59, line 24, I asked about the topic of their conversation when he saw him. And I also had a subquestion about Colonel Gagovic, who he was, he was the fourth member in that conversation, and I believe that my questions follow a logical sequence and that the witness is answering accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the question that caused Mr. Harmon to rise is the question that said: "What was Colonel Gagovic's position at the time?" It was not the question about -- sorry, I'm going to have to -- it was not the question about: "Did you talk to him on that occasion; if you did, what was the topic of your conversation? In answer to that question he said: "We entered a room, or rather, an office in the 4th Corps command in Lukavica. There were Kukanjac, General Mladic, Colonel Gagovic, and myself..." At that point you should have insisted that he answer your question: What did you talk about? He must answer that question before you then next ask the next question. Because now if he's going to answer this question after you've asked the next question, then we get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, however, wouldn't it be even more confusing for you if you didn't know who Gagovic was? I just wanted to clarify who the fourth member in the conversation was. Gagovic was mentioned and that's why I had that subquestion as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you must organise your questions in your mind in that manner. You are going to ask him who Gagovic was, and then after asking him that, I'm going to ask him what they talked about. Otherwise, if he's now going to tell us who Gagovic was when he's supposed to be telling us what they talked about, then that causes confusion. And it's important -- I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic, it's very important, one, to listen to yourself and listen to your own questions; and listen clearly to the answer from the witness and check whether he's answering your question. And if he's not, insist on getting the answer. It's just so important for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not trying to create even more confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I had reasons for that additional question, and I believe that I'm following the sequence of what I wanted to ask the witness. But let's try and be as economical and as up to the point as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. You may try that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, what was the subject of that conversation with Kukanjac, Mladic, and Gagovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: General Kukanjac briefly told us about the massacre at Dobrovoljacka Street. General Mladic offered me the post of commander of the 4th Corps, replacing General Djurdjevac who was leaving that position because he originally hailed from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mladic tell you what would become of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. It was only about this vacancy created by the corps commander leaving his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with General Mladic's position at the time? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew from the media - and he said so himself - he said that the VRS had been established and that he had been appointed commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. He said he had the power to appoint me to an appropriate position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "an appropriate position," given the nature of his speech and given the nature of his position in the VRS, what exactly was the position you thought he was alluding to and in which army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: He offered me the post of commander of the 4th Corps of the JNA, which in the meantime had been renamed and was now called the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. When this corps became part of the VRS, it got its new name and went by that name for the rest of the war, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He offered me the post of commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your reply?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I turned the offer down and I explained my refusal. I said I was unable to take up any duty in any army until I was able to evacuate my family from Sarajevo, and Sarajevo at the time was under siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity here. This position that he offered you in the 4th Corps of the JNA you say is the same thing as the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So he was offering you that post. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before August, when your family was eventually able to leave Sarajevo, did you travel to Belgrade -- or rather, let's do it this way. What did your information at the time suggest regarding the position of former JNA officers who hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to this creation of a new army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had the same information that was available and known to all JNA officers, all JNA members, leaving the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as those who were staying. The most important information was this: All JNA members originally hailing from BH territory, as well as volunteers who stay on in the VRS and are members of the former JNA, would have their social status arranged as planned and envisaged by the political leaders on the one hand of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the leadership of the former Presidency of the SFRY. That the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the legal heir to the former JNA and on those grounds and pursuant to that agreement and contract between countries, a solution was drawn up for all members of the former JNA who remained in the VRS, to have their salaries guaranteed as well as their pension and health benefits and years of service, that would be honoured in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under the authority of the Supreme Defence Council and the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say all former members of the JNA. Was this about all of them or about only a specific category of former JNA members?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Officers and NCOs, those two categories alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also say that an agreement was drawn up. You mention the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When you say "agreement," do you know if they actually agreed this with anyone or was that their call and their decision and no one else's? What does your information suggest, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the agreement involved the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, above all Alija Izetbegovic, because that agreement was meant to regulate or to settle the status of officers and NCOs from the former JNA, I mean those who joined the BH army on the one hand and the HVO on the other. The agreement, as far as I know, was reached between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the then-internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The agreement was co-signed by the representatives of the authorities belonging to all the three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What became of the former members, officers, and NCOs of the JNA who joined the BH army or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to that agreement, they were free to choose whether they would be joining the VJ and receiving their salaries there, the alternative being to stay with the BH army and receive their salaries from Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the following proviso. Those persons who have reached retirement age and sufficient years of service, regardless of whether they were Muslims or Croats but were members of the JNA, were now entitled to collect their pensions from Yugoslavia or indeed to give it up and collect their pensions from Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why the agreement was reached at the level of the two countries involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you actually see this agreement? Where do you get your information on the agreement from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not myself read the actual agreement. Nevertheless, whenever this subject was raised at the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska meeting, this agreement was always invoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska later on. I suppose you're saying this in relation to the time that you were a member of the Supreme Command. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, just to make sure we can follow what you're saying, what was the time-period you were talking about? When were you a member of the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Having been appointed defence minister, I automatically became a member of the Supreme Command by virtue of my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll discuss that later at quite some length. Do you know whether there was anything in the media or elsewhere about the leadership of Republika Srpska calling on former JNA officers who originally hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina to join the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the period before you were able to get your family out of Sarajevo, did you travel to Belgrade between August 1992 and May 1992 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've probably managed to mix things up a little. Can you please tell us, General, where did you go and who did you see and when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I got in touch with General Sljivic, chief of the technical administration of the SSM in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in June 1992, sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Having learned about my fate, he offered me a post implying the rank of general in the VJ specifically to be located in Podgorica, Podgorica garrison. I refused and explained that I was unable to accept any appointment anywhere at all, whatever the offer. The first thing I had to make sure was my family was safely out of Sarajevo because they were trapped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When did your family finally make it out of Sarajevo? We don't need to get the date right, but roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 9th of July, or possibly the 9th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened after that -- or rather, can you tell us first where you put your family up for the rest of the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I put them up with friends who were in Pale. They spent some time on my own property, which could not be used for actually living there through the winter. I managed to get the appropriate documents for my daughter to be able to continue her education over in Belgrade. Sometime in late August I took my family to Belgrade and put them up with my sister and her husband in Belgrade at --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, but were they there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly in Belgrade. Later on my wife also spent some time with me in Pale, during the war and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what became of your flat in Sarajevo, very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a flat that I owned. It had been bought. There was a valid contract certified by a court. The procedure was perfectly fair. The flat has not been returned to me to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see General Mladic again after that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mladic on several occasions. I pleaded with him to help me get my family out of Sarajevo. In that respect, there was nothing he could do for me or at least that's what he said. Nevertheless, he did ask me to take up a post to be determined by him at the Main Staff of the VRS, saying this would be something to do with logistics and that I would be working with General Djukic. Again, I refused until I was able to make sure my family was safe. He then went on to tell me -- each and every time he told me, in fact, that he would ask for me not to be appointed to the VJ but to the VRS instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was he going to address with that regard? Who was he going to ask for that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who he meant, but I suppose that he meant the supreme council -- Supreme Defence Council, which was in charge of such matters, of adopting the decision for me as well as for all those who had been appointed to the Main Staff and the Army of Republika Srpska up to then, the decision on my status, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what the status of those officers in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was their status regulated, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic told me personally -- on several occasions he explained that to me. He told me that my status would be dealt with in Yugoslavia, just like mine is, Milovanovic's, Gvero's, Djukic's and others. And he explained that inter-state agreement in quite some detail. He had read it in Belgrade while he was with President Milosevic's office and other leaders of the then-Yugoslavia. He said that that was a solution for them and that it would also be for me if we all accepted to be paid from Yugoslavia to have our social security and medical benefits in Yugoslavia, that our pensionable years of service are counted in Yugoslavia. And all that time we would be members of the Army of Republika Srpska, exclusively of that army and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you were offered to be a member of the logistics sector with General Djukic. Did you know General Djukic from before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him well. He was in Belgrade and he attended a few professional seminars and meetings, and that's when I saw him and had a few occasions to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mladic tell you why he kept on insisting on you joining the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you share that with us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When members of the former JNA joined the VJ, I was the only logistics man who hailed from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was familiar with the entire infrastructure to the very last detail, since I had worked in the area for 20 years before then. If General Djukic, his logistics assistant, had arrived from Belgrade, if he -- actually, he said that Djukic arrived from Belgrade and he did not know anything about the infrastructure, the depots, the units, he didn't know anything and everything was completely new, both for him and for everybody else; and I, on the other hand, was familiar with everything, not only familiar but I knew it like the back of my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time when you joined and when you became a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I wrote to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and in my letter I stated my requests and I said I will take up a position in the Main Staff of the VRS on a condition that my status was dealt with in Yugoslavia, just like it was for the rest of the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get in touch with anybody from the personnel administration of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not get in touch with anybody before I received an answer to my written request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Could you please tell us about that answer, when did you receive it and what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mladic told me that my request was accepted and that my status would be resolved in Yugoslavia, and based on my letter of acceptance he issued an order on my appointment as a member of the Main Staff of the VRS. My position was not defined at the time; however, I worked in the logistics sector with General Djukic and I considered myself a desk officer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the previous question. After you received that information from Mladic, did you get in touch with somebody from the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Through the personnel administration of the Main Staff of the VRS, I was asked to go and sign a document in the personnel administration, a document which was my acceptance of my status being arranged in the Army of Yugoslavia, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try and avoid any confusion. I asked you whether you got in touch with anybody from the Army of Yugoslavia, and you said that through the personnel administration of the VRS you got in touch with the personnel administration of the Army of Yugoslavia. Did I understand your question [as interpreted] properly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I personally never got in touch with the personnel administration or the Army of Yugoslavia with regard to my status. That was done on my behalf by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: And when that status was finally resolved, the personnel administration of the Main Staff of the VRS informed me that I should go to the personnel administration of the Army of Yugoslavia to sign a document which was the decision on my status in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, as we heard at the beginning of your testimony, you hail from Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the former VJ -- JNA officers who hailed from Croatia, in respect of what you have just told us about Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Again, General Mladic provided me with the details of that. When he tried to persuade me to stay, or rather, join the Army of Republika Srpska, he then told me that the position of the leadership of Yugoslavia was for all members of the JNA who hailed from Croatia should join the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina; and all those who were born on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to join the Army of Republika Srpska. Based on their place of birth, they were supposed to participate in the defence system and the defence of their territories, peoples, houses, friends, and relatives. I was told that irrespective of my status being arranged in Yugoslavia, I could only be a member of the VRS or of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina. And based on those two offers, I had a long thought and finally I made a decision based on the elements that I've already shared with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, you were faced with two options. How did you finally decide to respond to Ratko Mladic's invitation, to respond positively to that invitation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were a few elements that went into that. First of all, I wanted to remain a career officer. I wanted to remain with the Army of Republika Srpska because I knew everything very well, like the back of my hand. Wherever I went elsewhere, everything would be new, and it was very uncertain how I would fare in the war-struck areas elsewhere in other positions and discharging other duties. The second reason was purely humane and patriotic, the relationship that I had and my officers' honour that compelled me to stay with the people that I belonged to. And that's why I had to participate together with them with the system of defence and to help them defend themselves in the territory where they were threatened. I couldn't allow myself to leave to go to Yugoslavia and to become a deserter and perceived as such by my relatives, friends, and family. I had my old parents residing in the territory of Croatia. They were living alone, threatened by the war, and I didn't think it would be humane for me to leave them, that it was my duty and obligation to look after them and to participate in their defence and a rescue operation, if need be, of both of them and the property that was very valuable. I had property in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, also relatively valuable. That was my private property. And I realised that I would lose all that unless I stayed in the territory, unless I protected all that with my own presence there. All of these elements made me join the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, if need be, and when I wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And which one did you join, if any at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just said on two different occasions, I accepted a position in the Army of Republika Srpska, in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, whose commander was General Mladic; and I was subordinated to General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what duties did you discharge in the Main Staff in the logistics sector? I suppose that you joined the logistics sector as soon as you said that you were subordinated to Djukic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At that time we had a major task to establish the units and institutions of the Army of Republika Srpska. I was appointed as a member of the commission of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska headed by an operative, Colonel Ilic. An order to establish that commission which also defined the task of that commission had been signed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. So what was the task of that commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The task of that commission was inspect all the units and institutions of the Army of Republika Srpska in the entire territory, also to assist with the establishment of units. I, as a logistics man, and the others were tasked with preventing paramilitaries from existing within the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, any paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was logistics organised in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At first there were different ways to do that and there were a lot of problems. Later on some order was installed; however, in principle every brigade had its own logistics support and its own reserves. Every corps had its own logistics support unit and its own reserves. The Main Staff of the VRS had under its command logistics bases and repair and overhaul institutions which it commanded directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many logistics bases of the VRS army there were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were three, perhaps four, but I would say that there were three rather than four.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the 774th Logistics Base of the JNA, what happened to it, the one that had existed up to the 1990s, the beginning of the 1990s? Okay, let's not pin-point a date. What happened to the base?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When the Army of Republika Srpska was established - and I believe that that was on the 12th of May, 1992 - the Main Staff renamed that logistics base and its new name was the 27th Logistics Base; and its command was in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be very precise. The 27th Logistics Base of what army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what does it mean when you say that the three or four logistics bases were -- let's say, 27th Logistics Base were subordinated to the Main Staff, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just correct your first question. There was a logistics base in Banja Luka, there was one in Bijeljina, the 30th was in Bileca, and the 27th was in Sokolac. In other words, there were four logistics bases, and now can you repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that they were subordinated to the Main Staff. Now we have heard that there were definitely four of them. What does it mean when you say that they were subordinated to the Main Staff? What does it mean? Who could come to a logistics base and take anything from any of them? A very simple question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the rules and regulations as well as the orders and the Law on the Army, only the Main Staff could issue an order for any of the logistics bases to issue from their depots some materiel or equipment to any of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska or anybody else for that matter. And the same applied to the receipt of such materiel and equipment in the depots of the logistics bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you've just put us in the picture, as it were, as to how this equipment was distributed from brigade level all the way up to the Main Staff. I'll now go back to the brigade that you mentioned a while ago. When you toured those units at the time, what did you observe as far as your own sector, logistics, was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I observed several important things, important for me and important for the Main Staff. Firstly, most battalion- and brigade-level were part of the JNA and became part of the JNA as TO units belonging to Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said "became part of the JNA," I think that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Became part of the VRS. That's what I meant to say. As members of the Serb TO and as volunteer units who had been classified up until that point in time as volunteers. Nevertheless, they all agreed to sport VRS insignia and to carry out the orders given by their superior officers in the chain of command of the VRS. As for them having their own depots full of ammunition, weapons, and military equipment, most of all those weapons and equipment had been taken or captured from the JNA when they withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Or else depots under the control of the Serb side were attacked, taken, all of the equipment and weapons being seized. That was -- there was a dramatic example of that in Rudo, in Visegrad, in Ustikolina, Manje [phoen], Vardiste, and for the most part Foca. Next, they didn't allow for those weapons and the reserves to be duly registered. I myself in a technical sense inspected all of the rear units. They were poorly qualified. They didn't know how to keep their files or records. They had no records at all. What that amounted to in their case was making notes in common notebooks, but only what the local commander allowed them to actually list. Whatever he considered to be his own reserve he would refuse to have recorded or registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "whatever he considered to be his own reserve," can you please elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In such cases I would always step in and ask commanders to write down every single bullet, every single piece of equipment, and have it recorded and registered and categorised. And he said, "No way. I was the one who got this, I was the one who seized this, and there's no one who can take it away from me whatever you think you can do about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as the work of this commission is concerned, did you ever inform the Main Staff about these facts or whoever requested a report from you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The first tour that I made took just over a month. We drew up a joint report. In that report I provided a detailed description of all these difficulties. I also put forward the proposal that the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS should use the chain of command to exercise his power and issue appropriate orders, for everything to be listed and everything to be recorded, also that the command system should be observed from the Main Staff level to the lowliest unit in order to prevent any interference by local authorities in terms of the command system and the supply system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Can you please explain this, I'm looking at something that I'm interested in, something you mentioned, "interference by local authorities in ... the command system ..." What exactly did you mean by that, what did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA local authorities -- or Serbian Democratic Party local authorities wanted to establish absolute control over brigades that were established in their own municipal territories in every respect including the command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These brigades now formally part of the VRS, are those the ones you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of the VRS and that's exactly what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did they want to go about establishing their authority over these units?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to be the ones to issue combat orders to these units in terms of what each of the brigades would be defending or attacking, seizing, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did they actually manage to exert any influence over these matters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to quite a considerable extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did the Main Staff do about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I know that Mladic issued some orders, but the approach they took was a benevolent one. Had it not been for the local authorities and their assistance, they would not have been able to establish an army; that is what they believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit D50 for a moment. Thank you. This is a 1st Krajina Corps document, the 22nd of February [sic], 1993, signed by General Talic. We'll wait up for the English to appear on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this document speaks for itself, at least the first portion does. Nevertheless, it's the third paragraph that I'm looking at and I would like to have your comment. There is a reference there to donors in municipalities located in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps. What exactly is General Talic implying there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This document is a faithful reflection of the situation. Commander General Talic requests that the Government of Republika Srpska or the Main Staff purchase these specified amounts of ammunition or else that he be allowed to gather funds from donors in order to wrap up this job as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What I want to know is this: We're talking about the local level and when we say "donors," who exactly were they and how could they get funds for purchasing ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The local-level authorities, such as municipal authorities, were the most important and for the most part permanent donors to their local units, normally brigade-level units. In terms of the role of the political authorities, donors were identified who in this case were wealthy entrepreneurs. The political authorities ordered them to trade and purchase various kinds of goods for the purposes of the VRS, saying that they would be remunerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll be addressing that at a later stage, but what I'm looking at now is the local level. General, are you familiar with the situation concerning the influence of the local authorities over the units and these local-level donations, so to speak? This was the case in 1993, but did that continue throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Throughout the war, from the very start of the war and all the way up to the signing of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a P exhibit, P1067.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a later document from 1995, but I just want to know about the procedure that we discussed a while ago when we spoke about the respective authorities and powers, who was in charge of what. Can you please comment on that -- on this document in terms of procurement and how ammunition was supplied that came to be in certain depots.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This document reflects a procedure. This was the official procedure. The VRS Main Staff orders its own subordinate bases, specifically the 27th Logistics Base, to issue these types of ammunition to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. At the same time, the Pretis Vogosca company was supposed to be involved in this and issue certain types of goods pursuant to this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the delivery order there is a reference to the 27th Logistics Base, and you say there were a total of four of those. Do those bases cover certain corps in a territorial sense? For example, could the Krajina Corps go to the 27th Logistics Base? How exactly was that organised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, the logistics bases were not related to any specific corps. All of the bases catered to all of the units in the VRS. As a matter of principle, though, the infrastructure of individual bases simply happened to be wherever it was. And if there was a corps nearby, they would normally rely on that base. Nevertheless, all of the bases had the same commitment under the orders of the Main Staff, to issue goods or receive goods and equipment from any unit in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see that there is a section of this document that is highlighted because someone found it relevant. There is mention there of Pretis and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command being able to retrieve their ammunition directly from Pretis. We'll talk about Pretis later on. Nevertheless, could the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps get their ammunition directly from Pretis without previously receiving authorisation from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could and that was one of the difficulties that I faced in my work as minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why is that? Why was that a difficulty?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Simply because sometimes General Mladic would go to Pretis. He would order the Pretis manager to cease all supplies to anyone at all, also saying that production should continue only in relation to the unit that he specified. He would bring his security there and would often threaten the manager that he would either be removed, replaced, or liquidated. He forced Pretis to produce ammunition for a particular unit. This practice was also employed by some local commanders of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They knew that if a platoon went there or a considerable number of armed soldiers led by a commander, they would simply lay siege to the production line, wait for the eventual product, they would simply take it, load it onto their vehicles, and be off. This kind of information was shared with me by the Pretis manager. This was the reason that we were never able to set up and maintain a production and financing as normal. There was always someone who came along and took something away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have probably come straight to the matter too soon, but let me ask you: The purpose production industry Republika Srpska, who was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All purpose industry companies were part of the ministry of the industry and the Government of Republika Srpska as state companies. The Ministry of Defence had the authority and possibility to commission works from such companies and order goods required by the Army of Republika Srpska, including ammunition. But that was based on production contracts and those services had to be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let's come back to the work of your commission and let's round the topic off. When you inspected all of those units, what impression did you gain about the equality of the distribution of the ammunition among the units of Republika Srpska? Did everybody have the same or were there any differences?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the local level, the distribution was even, whereas at high levels, at the levels of -- level of brigades and corps, the distribution was not even; some had more and some had much less and some had even too much, far too much. The inner command of the Main Staff of the VRS considered that report, General Mladic, General Milovanovic, and General Djukic primarily, and they decided who to take the surplus from and who to give it to. They were the ones who were in charge of the distribution, and it was General Djukic who then told me or issued me orders to draft documents together with my service, to draft orders and instructions that would follow the same line as the previous ones. Those orders were signed either by Mladic or General Milovanovic. And for some equipment such orders could be signed also by General Djukic. And then the equipment and materiel was distributed among the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is the time, Your Honour, to finish today's sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Kovacevic, we are not able to finish with you today. You'll have to come back tomorrow, but while you are out and not in court, until you finish testifying, just to warn you, you are not allowed to discuss the case with anybody. Okay. And we sit tomorrow in the morning at 9.00, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
